en: The Sūtra on the Pure Method of Observing the Fast Spoken by the Buddha.

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery together with two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings.
When the spirits, devas, bodhisattvas,
and mahāsattvas had assembled together at one time,
Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat.
He prostrated himself before the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One."
In the past, when I entered the city to beg for alms,
I encountered on the road several tens of thousands of people whose heads were as large as Mount Tai.
His belly was like Mount Sumeru,
his throat and neck were like needles,
and when he walked, his footsteps made a sound like five hundred chariots.
The smoke issues forth from his mouth;
by what offense has this been caused?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound this for me.
The Buddha said,
"Alas, alas! He addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:"
As for these hungry ghosts:
in a previous life, they prepared vegetarian offerings for a feast and, after the meal was finished, broke the precepts in the afternoon;
consequently, they have now received such a retribution.
Even one who consumes another's vegetarian feast (śīla-āhāra) without themselves observing the fast shall receive this retribution.
Once the feast has concluded,
whatever remains of the food must not be given indiscriminately to those who do not observe the fast.
After the meal has been finished and the formal recitation completed, the donor should announce:
"May the assembly of monks please accept my gift with joy.
Whatever food remains, the assembly of monks should bestow it upon the disciples.
Thereafter, one may joyfully use it according to one's own wishes.
If one does not consult the Sangha, both the recipient and the donor incur fault.
Maudgalyāyana replied:
It is indeed as the holy teaching states.
The Buddha said:
"All the requisites for the Dharma assemblies and vegetarian feasts provided by donors."
If one is able to observe the fast, they may receive this food;
if one does not observe the fast, they must not eat it at will.
To do so would incur immeasurable and boundless transgression.
If one can observe the fast for even a single day,
one will obtain surplus provisions for six million future lifetimes;
if one does not observe the fast while eating the food of those who do, [the merit will be lost].
For six hundred thousand lifetimes, one will fall among the hungry ghosts.
Why is this? Because this food is a heavy gift of faith.
It would be better to swallow a hot iron ball than to eat this rice.
To swallow a hot iron ball is but for a brief moment;
yet by consuming the food offered in faith by others, one undergoes suffering for a long time.
For five million lifetimes, they shall suffer the torments of hungry ghosts.
Whenever an assembly is convened,
let everyone perform the ritual offerings according to the Dharma.
One must not harbor any remaining scraps;
instead, one should give them to one's friends and kinsmen to eat this cake and rice.
If one harbors even a trace of residual malice,
for five million lifetimes they shall dwell within the hells,
where hot iron wheels pass back and forth across their armpits and flanks.
They will suffer great agony as their bodies are scorched and consumed.
One must be extremely careful regarding all food for the fast;
even a single grain of rice or wheat can transform into a glowing iron ball.
Whenever any donor intends to establish a merit-gathering assembly,
those who have already tasted this food beforehand have all consumed leftovers; thus,
holding such an assembly would be in vain.
"It is better not to do it at all. Why?
Because the devas and spirits would not be pleased."
This person, having previously tasted the sacrificial offerings,
shall likewise suffer the torments of a hungry ghost for five million lifetimes.
From this day forward, those who desire to obtain merit [should abstain].
It is best to purify oneself according to the aforementioned method;
having washed the hands and body of flour and chaff,
one should first establish it in a secluded place.
Do not conceal the coverings or taste the offerings.
If you perform the *zhāi* (fasting/feast) according to the Dharma, you shall obtain blessings and merit,
and the various devas will rejoice.
The hundred deities rejoice;
benevolent spirits provide protection.
The sutra does not speak falsely.
Karmic retribution is like a shadow or an echo.
This hungry ghost originally came from the human realm;
because he touched the robes and bowls of the Sangha with impure hands, [he has now suffered this fate].
With unclean hands, they defile the pure food of the śramaṇas;
with unclean hands, they place [impurities] into the food of the śramaṇas;
and with such unclean food, they intend to offer it to the Saṅgha as well as to their parents.
In the subsequent five hundred years, they will fall among the hungry ghosts (preta),
constantly eating impurities;
when they first wish to go to the latrine to consume excrement and urine, they [will find it blocked].
Then that toilet deity, holding an iron staff in his hand,
prevents those hungry ghosts from approaching the latrine;
they constantly consume pus, blood, mucus, saliva, and the foul liquid used for cleaning.
Constantly taking as their sustenance the foul impurities of women who have given birth and the blood-stained filth,
they further pass through five million lifetimes falling among swine, pigs, and dung beetles.
They constantly consume foul, filthy, and impure things;
undergoing such bitter suffering for successive generations,
they endure toil and hardship for many tens of millions of kalpas with no prospect of escape.
It is difficult to attain liberation;
the pain is beyond description.
Sometimes they touch their own bodies with their hands, such as the male or female organs and so forth.
Or if one uses this hand to touch the pure food of a śramaṇa or one’s parents,
or places impure food upon it to give to a śramaṇa or one’s parents,
one shall incur this calamity.
All those with physical eyes cannot discern sin or merit.
From this day forward, if you wish to receive assistance from the Sangha when preparing meals, [you must act accordingly].
With clean hands and body, one should hold the food vessels of the Saṃgha;
with clean hands, one should pour out the rice and flour,
and prepare the meal with pure water.
One shall obtain immeasurable merit.
From this day forward, let it be widely proclaimed so that all may hear and know it,
and practice according to what has been taught.
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha,
"I shall propagate it;
I dare not forget it."
Practicing with a sincere mind.
The Sūtra on the Pure Method of Observing the Fast Spoken by the Buddha.
